articles.title: Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history
articles.summary: Two analytics firms have attributed the incident to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters By Osmond Chia ,  Business reporter   and   Angus Thompson 
- Published 30 October 2026 
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record. 
The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses". 
The company said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach". 
Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor. 
Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack. 
Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record". 
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack. 
The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen. 
The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added. 
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide. 
The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody. 
The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world. 
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack. 
For the last few years North Korea-linked operatives have focussed on attacking cryptocurrency companies for large thefts of digital tokens. 
Western security agencies have previously said stolen funds are used to finance North Korea's nuclear weapons and missile development programs. 
The regime has denied any involvement in hacks in the past. 
Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets. 
Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." 
The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue. 
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop. 
"That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions," he said in a statement. 
"To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual. So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak." 
He said a detailed "post-mortem" would be shared once the investigation was complete. 
In an update, the company said in a statement on X that another investigation found there had been other breach points: "We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them." 
Check Point's Dave said this attack also resembled a hack on crypto exchange platform Bitget in September in which $388m (£289m) was lost: "This implies that attackers no longer need the vault keys. They target the systems and people with authority to use them." 
In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets. 
"Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said. 
Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack. 
World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds. 
Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation. 
Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue. 
Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.

articles.title: China made Mbappé apologise - but many don't know exactly what he said
articles.summary: His comment about Chinese leader Mao sparked anger but censorship left many wondering what exactly happened.
articles.full_text:
Image source, CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images By Fan Wang 
- Published 29 October 2026 
On Monday night, as Kylian Mbappé was attending the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London, he was also becoming the centre of a huge controversy on Chinese social media. 
Football fans had stumbled upon a clip of him joking about the meme that makes him "laugh the most" - where his face is superimposed on a "Chinese dictator" resembling Mao Zedong, who oversaw one of the bloodiest chapters in the country's past. 
The controversy spread like wildfire as Chinese brands cut him off one by one and China Media Group, the parent group of state broadcaster CCTV, suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches. A foreign ministry spokesperson said: "Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society." 
But on the Chinese internet, few were explicitly spelling out those words and actions, or even using the name of Mao - who remains a near-sacred figure in the country. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: The Mbappé-Chairman Mao controversy explained 
China's sophisticated censorship system, which cuts 1.4 billion people off from the global internet, meant many didn't know exactly what had happened. 
The accusation of "hurting the feelings of the Chinese people" alone seemed enough to trigger a tsunami of anger, amplified by social media algorithms and a heavily controlled internet, where people are wary of disagreeing with the majority view. 
It wasn't long before Mbappé, one of the biggest football stars in the world, said he was "sincerely sorry" for his "ill-judged" comment . His club, Real Madrid, and the Spanish league La Liga, also issued apologies. China is a huge market for the world's most popular sport. 
Beijing later confirmed it was taking the footballer's apology "seriously". China Media Group has yet to say whether broadcasts will resume. 
But the anger online lingered. 
"An apology is the least he should do, but I don't forgive him. I support a ban on him," read a top comment on Weibo. 
Mbappé did not mention Mao by name in the interview, but many felt any joke that involved the founder of Communist China crossed a line. 
"Do you know who you hurt? He is the spiritual pillar of the Chinese people," read one Weibo comment liked by more than 700 users. 
"He's the most important figure in our history. Do you think a simple apology can make everything okay?" another wrote. 
Image source, Weibo Image caption, 
Weibo users shared the clip by blurring the meme and redacting references to Mao 
Ironically, despite the heavy backlash, many on Chinese social media are still asking what exactly the French forward said. They tried AI chatbots, which are just as censored as the Chinese internet and couldn't provide any answers. Others attempted to explain, but skirted around any mention of Mao. 
References were made to "the person on the 100 yuan note" and "the teacher", a title Mao once used for himself. Screenshots of the meme and interview were shared, with both the word "dictator" and Mbappé's face blurred out. 
Neither the Chinese foreign ministry statement nor the apologies issued by Mbappé, Real Madrid and La Liga mentioned Mao directly. 
Mao, who led the Chinese Communist Party to victory in the civil war and founded the People's Republic of China, died in 1976. 
Despite the turmoil of his rule, including the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which led to a famine that killed tens of millions and unleashed violent purges across Chinese society, he remains a revered figure in China. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
It is illegal to "insult" or "slander" Communist Party martyrs and war heroes in China 
A portrait of Mao overlooks Beijing's Tiananmen Square, a symbol of how central he is in the modern Chinese imagination. Unlike other former Chinese leaders, his embalmed body is placed on public display there, drawing tens of thousands of visitors every day. In recent years, there has been a revival of interest in him among young people, who read his works and watch clips of him on social media. 
Chinese history books downplay the devastation during Mao's rule. The Chinese Communist Party's verdict on Mao is that his achievements outweigh his mistakes. In their eyes, he is "a great revolutionary and a great Marxist". 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Mbappe's Chinese social media Weibo account was banned from being followed by new users on Tuesday 
But outside China, history sees Mao as both a revolutionary and a dictator. And so reactions among the diaspora - dissidents as well as people whose families fled China decades ago, in the wake of Mao's rule - was very different. 
"You don't need to apologise, you are not wrong," a highly liked comment written in Chinese under the football star's X statement read. 
"The ones who should apologise are the CCP; they kidnapped the Chinese people and brainwashed them," another Chinese user wrote. 
On X and Threads, neither of which are accessible in China, the controversy spawned even more memes. Some feature Mbappé's face on other images of Mao, while others go further, placing him on the body of current Chinese leader Xi Jinping. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Dairy company Mengniu, an official sponsor of the Fifa World Cup, cut ties with the footballer after the backlash 
And then there was the rest of the internet which was simply puzzled. 
"It's honestly hard to understand... It seems like people aren't allowed to speak out against their leaders. And they expect the whole world to think the same way they do? That's ridiculous," read a top comment under Real Madrid's apology on Instagram. 
"How dare you call a dictator a dictator? Terrible," another user on X wrote.

articles.title: Hong Kong's leader apologises for deadly high-rise fire
articles.summary: The massive blaze at Wang Fuk Court in November 2025 was the deadliest the city had seen in decades.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
John Lee (centre) bowed in apology along with top officials By Tessa Wong 
- Published 29 October 2026 
The chief executive of Hong Kong, John Lee, has apologised for a massive fire that ripped through an apartment complex last year and killed 168 people. 
Speaking at a press conference, Lee promised major reforms to government departments to ensure such an incident would not happen again. 
A report by an independent committee, released by the government at the press conference, found that the fire was caused by "misconduct" by the private sector as well as "decades of failure" by government bodies. 
The massive blaze at Wang Fuk Court in November 2025 was the deadliest the city had seen in decades. Dozens of people have been arrested on suspicion of manslaughter, fraud or corruption. 
At the start of the press conference on Thursday, John Lee said he was "deeply sorrowful" about the fire and that on behalf of his government, "I apologise to the victims as well as the city's residents". 
He then stood up and bowed, along with several top officials. 
Later he announced that the city's housing secretary Winnie Ho had resigned to take accountability for the fire. 
The independent committee's report found that the fire was most likely caused by a "glowing source, likely a cigarette" which ignited "paper materials" at the apartment complex, which was undergoing extensive renovation at the time. 
Officials have said the government may start using AI and drones with infra-red cameras to detect and identify smokers on construction sites. 
The report also found that the construction companies in charge of the renovation used sub-standard building materials and had unsafe procedures. 
This included using scaffolding nets that were not fire retardant and covering up windows with inflammable foam boards for a prolonged period of time. 
The companies had also used fake information in paperwork to "feign compliance" with regulators' rules, according to the report. 
The committee said the main contractor and consultant for the renovation, as well as several individuals associated with the project, deserved "the most severe criticisms" for the fire. 
But had the various government departments involved in the project possessed a "sense of crisis" and "paid sufficient heed" to the possibility of misconduct, it added, such behaviour as well as the fire hazards at Wang Fuk Court could have been rectified. 
The report also said there were "widespread, systematic and long-standing" practices in the construction sector that were "unlawful and dubious". There was also bid-rigging and other misconduct by various parties, including some who had connections with local mafias, it said. 
Lee said that the various government bodies involved in the case would be investigated, and that a unit in the housing bureau which conducts independent checks would be replaced. 
Lee also promised to crack down on bid-rigging, including criminalising the practice, and introduce long jail terms and heavy fines. 
Built in the 1980s, Wang Fuk Court in Hong Kong's north-eastern Tai Po district housed about 4,600 people. 
Nearly 40% of the residents were 65 or older, and many of the fire's victims were elderly people. 
Thousands of firefighters were deployed to bring the fire under control. One of them, 37-year-old Ho Wai-ho, died during the firefighting operation. 
The fire deeply shocked and worried Hong Kong, a densely populated city where many residents live in similar ageing high-rises, and sparked calls for accountability.

articles.title: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
articles.summary: Xi's anti-corruption campaign has become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", observers say.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
This is the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300 By Kelly Ng   and   Ian Tang ,  BBC Monitoring 
- Published 29 October 2026 Updated 30 October 2026 
A record 33 members have been expelled from China's Communist Party as it concluded a major annual political gathering, which had the most empty seats ever seen. 
The fifth plenum was attended by 279 Central Committee members, compared to 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third one in July 2024. 
While recent plenums focused on economic reforms or social and development issues, party discipline took centre stage at this week's gathering. 
Xi Jinping has made the fight against corruption a central pillar of his rule since he took the reins in 2012, calling it the "biggest threat" to the party. 
Since then, more than two million individuals have been disciplined for cases related to "pointless formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance", Zhang Fuhai, from the party's disciplinary commission, told a press briefing on Friday. 
He also said the party would enhance its efforts to ensure officials "dare not, cannot, and do not want to be corrupt". 
Anti-corruption purges continue 
Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing. 
It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign. 
It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China. 
"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption." 
In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollowed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder". 
The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 35 and five in his first and second terms respectively. 
Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year. 
This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members. 
Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty. 
In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The party says it's going after "pointless formalities", which inlcude "bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance" 
Who are the key figures purged? 
Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violated [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption. 
The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own". 
"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote. 
Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman. 
Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-man Politburo was at one point left with 21 members. 
Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22. 
Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged. 
"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment." 
Xi's plans for the future 
Analysts believe one reason for the increased emphasis on discipline – which many interpret as loyalty – is next year's Party Congress, when the CCP will vote again for its next leader. 
A leadership reshuffle is due in 2027 and many analysts expect Xi to hold on to the top job for a fourth term and beyond. No leader has served that long except Mao Zedong, the founder of Communist China. 
Xi has reason to "scrutinise the next cohort more closely" given the fall of so many officials from the current committee, Thomas says. 
"Today's rising stars tend to be relatively young, boast technocratic backgrounds, and have connections to Xi's political network," he says, adding that "provincial leadership ranks are a promising place to look". 
Observers say that ultimately, Xi is expected to dominate personnel selection at the 21st Party Congress, which will further cement his grip on the party and the country. 
"Xi's focus is further consolidating power around himself... The readout from the plenum suggests he intends to be at the centre of China and the Communist Party for the foreseeable future," Chong says. 
"However, further down the road, such concentration of power may pave the way for a more serious power vacuum when Xi ages and slows down."

articles.title: Hello Kitty maker cuts ties with Japanese spy drama after China backlash
articles.summary: Sanrio has apologised after its merchandise line with Japanese TV series Vivant drew criticism.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Sanrio says it will strengthen review processes for future collaborations By Koh Ewe 
- Published 29 October 2026 
Sanrio, the company behind Hello Kitty, has apologised and ended its merchandise partnership with a controversial Japanese TV show after drawing backlash in China. 
Vivant, a popular spy thriller, has been widely slammed in Chinese state media and by Chinese social media users for its depiction of Chinese agents using brutal torture tactics on a Japanese operative. 
The criticism has extended to the internationally beloved Hello Kitty and her friends, including My Melody and Cinnamoroll, who were featured in merchandise dressed as characters from the show. 
Sanrio said it terminated its collaboration with Vivant after determining that it "contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio's core values". 
"Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people," Sanrio said in the statement late on Wednesday. 
"We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects." 
China-Japan ties have plunged to their lowest point in years, since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan last November sparked a diplomatic firestorm. 
Responding to a question in parliament, Takaichi suggested that Japan would activate its self-defence force if China attacked Taiwan . 
Beijing has since been heaping pressure on Tokyo, from restricting rare earth exports to curbing tourism and even reclaiming its pandas . 
Takaichi told parliament earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and planned to watch them over the year-end holidays. 
State-run Global Times took aim at Sanrio on Wednesday, saying the hugely popular cat character "should not dance with Japan's right wing". 
Sanrio "stands to lose far more than short-term sales" by collaborating with "anti-China content", the Global Times article said. "The trust and emotional bond it has built up over a long time will also suffer." 
When asked about Sanrio's scrapped partnership with Vivant on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry said the incident should "serve as a warning to the international community and discerning people in Japan". 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Hello Kitty has been criticised on Chinese state media and Chinese social media 
Hello Kitty is not the only internationally beloved figure to have faced such wrath in China in recent days. 
Earlier this week, several Chinese brands dropped French footballer Kylian Mbappé over comments he had made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong - which he has since apologised for. 
Vivant is about a Japanese salaryman who finds himself entangled in an international web of crime and espionage. 
Its first season, which aired in 2023, was set in a fictional Central Asian country. Its second season, which premiered in July, features Chinese agents torturing a Japanese spy by cutting his fingers and stabbing his abdomen. 
Chinese state outlets, including CCTV, argued that these tactics "highly overlap" with those historically used by Japanese troops against the Chinese, and that the drama "distorts the truth". 
Masamine Ryuho, the president of Vivant's TV network TBS, said on Wednesday that the show was completely fictional and had no intentions of "disparaging any particular country".

articles.title: Mbappé sorry for 'ill-judged' Mao remark after backlash in China
articles.summary: The France star had referred to the former Chinese leader as a "dictator" during an interview about memes.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
A backlash has erupted on Chinese social media over Mbappé's comments on a "Chinese dictator" By Kelly Ng 
- Published 27 October 2026 
Kylian Mbappé has apologised for "ill-judged" comments he made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong which led to him being dropped by several Chinese brands. 
Mbappé had reportedly told French talk show The Bridge the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." He then laughs as the clip cuts to a meme showing his face superimposed on an image resembling Mao. 
The meme is part of a running joke about the Real Madrid forward being called a "dictator" because of his huge influence in football. 
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappé said in a statement. 
"I apologise to everyone my words have upset." 
Spain's La Liga also apologised, saying it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé's recent comments have caused among Chinese fans". 
The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his chaotic and often violent rule that left millions dead. 
A few people came out in support of him on Chinese social media, but that is a rare response given China's tightly controlled internet, where people are expected to toe the party and government line on sensitive topics. 
Few topics are as sensitive as Mao, which may explain why brands were so quick to terminate partnerships with a global sports star like Mbappé. 
The original video is not available on the show's YouTube channel, and it's unclear when the interview hosted by Real Madrid's Aurélien Tchouaméni first aired. In clips that have been circulating online, Mbappé does not identify Mao by name. He says he "uses [the meme] with friends all the time". 
The furore appeared to kick off on Monday night after Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people". 
Screengrabs of the clip and meme have since spread quickly on Chinese social media, with people echoing this sentiment and even calling for a boycott of both the French striker and his club, Real Madrid. 
But some have blurred the meme itself as well as the part of the comment they found offensive, when Mbappe refers to "a Chinese dictator". 
Dongqiudi said in its statement that it was "unable to translate" his comments because they were "offensive to China and the Chinese people". 
Many people are therefore also wondering what exactly Mbappe said and have responded to the angry posts and comments with questions, wanting to know more. 
Image source, Weibo Image caption, 
Weibo users are recirculating the clip by blurring the meme and redacting references to Mao 
What is the reaction in China? 
Chinese fans have been criticising Mbappé – who is popular in China and has huge brand endorsements – of "profiting from the Chinese market yet making remarks that offend the Chinese public". 
"International public figures, in particular, should show greater respect and sensitivity, as national sentiment must never be taken lightly," reads another comment on Weibo. 
As the anger online grew louder, Chinese brands began to cut ties, although they did not explicitly refer to the video. 
The country's largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people". 
Drinks giant Dongpeng issued a similar statement: "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments." 
According to state-owned newspaper The Global Times, state broadcaster CCTV's news apps will not feature content related to the French striker. CCTV will also stop showing La Liga matches, Chinese media reported on Tuesday. Real Madrid is one of 20 clubs that play in the Spanish football league and is the most decorated team with 36 league titles. 
China's foreign ministry has also weighed in, with spokesperson Lin Jian saying: "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society." 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Mbappé has a significant commercial presence in China 
China is a major market for international sports stars and homegrown brands have signed multimillion-dollar endorsement contracts with Mbappé, Norwegian striker Erling Haaland, and NBA player Stephen Curry. 
By 14:00 local time on Tuesday, five of the top 10 trending topics on Weibo centered on Mbappé, with the hashtag "multiple brands terminate partnerships with Mbappé" topping the list. 
"Don't ever come to China," read one of the top comments on Weibo. 
Why is Mao a sensitive topic? 
Mao founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled through tumultuous decades in the 1960s and 1970s. 
His attempt at rapid industrialisation, which he called the Great Leap Forward, led to a famine that killed tens of millions. Then came the Cultural Revolution: a violent purge of anyone seen as a threat to Communism, which included Chinese intellectuals, landowners, artists and often rivals within the Party. 
His death in 1976 brought a new era for China, which began to open its doors to the global economy. Even as the country moved away from Mao's rule, he continued to be hailed by the party as a national icon whose legacy was beyond reproach. 
So jokes or memes about Mao are seen not just as an insult to the party but also its closely-guarded narrative about the country's past. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Mbappé has said some of the memes "reveal a lack of political and human awareness" 
It's unclear when the Mbappé meme involving Mao began but his nickname, "the dictator", has made the striker the subject of many memes and jokes online. 
Mbappé is widely regarded as one of the best footballers in the world and has wielded significant influence at the clubs he has played for. His extraordinary speed, goalscoring ability and worldwide popularity have made him a global icon, attracting millions of fans, major sponsorship deals and media attention, with his influence extending into fashion, culture and business. 
In 2024, he sued a French influencer and kebab shop owner for using his name in the description of one of the shop's sandwiches, leading to more jokes about the nickname. 
France teammate Ousmane Dembele jumped on the trend during the 2026 World Cup, calling Mbappé Mobut – a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, for three decades. 
In an interview with France Football in September, Mbappé acknowledged the light-heartedness behind many of these memes, but said they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people". 
"There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history," he said. 
"Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life." 
Additional reporting by Fan Wang and Osmond Chia

articles.title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
articles.summary: The latest figures mark a major milestone as Beijing grapples with an ageing population.
articles.full_text:
Image source, VCG via Getty Images By Osmond Chia Business reporter 
- Published 27 October 2026 
Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said. 
Official data released in the last week , external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%. 
The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole. 
The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say. 
China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children . 
The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population. 
At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under. 
No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy. 
The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said. 
"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying. 
The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. 
It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Birth rates in China have been falling for years now 
China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy , which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015. 
The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested. 
The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said. 
But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows. 
Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said. 
Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year. 
Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures. 
The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier. 
The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited. 
Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants. 
It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

articles.title: India and China were easing tensions - then a border official spoke out
articles.summary: India-China ties were on a cautious recovery path until a border official’s remarks raised fresh doubts about ground realities.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
India and China have a fragile thaw in relations since the 2020 clashes By Anbarasan Ethirajan Global affairs correspondent 
- Published 28 October 2026 
For much of the past year, India-China relations appeared to be on a cautious path to recovery. 
The two countries have seen ups and downs in their ties over decades - especially over the disputed Himalayan frontier. 
But events of the past few days suggest that the thaw which has followed their most recent clashes in 2020 may be more fragile than it seems. 
The latest concerns began when India's border police chief said Chinese troops had returned to disputed areas along the Himalayan frontier in large numbers earlier this year, pitching tents several kilometres inside territory claimed by India. 
The remarks by Shatrujeet Singh Kapur, director general of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), have triggered a political controversy in Delhi. 
To begin with, such comments by serving officials are rare. Sensitive border issues are usually addressed by the federal government through its defence or foreign ministries. 
At a recent gathering of officers in Rajasthan state, Kapur said face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops had taken place at several locations in the north-eastern state of Arunachal Pradesh and were continuing. 
The confrontations began in July, he said, but both sides initially withdrew. 
A few days later, Chinese troops returned in larger numbers and pitched tents "around six-to-seven kilometres inside India's perception of the Line of Actual Control (LAC)", he added. 
The LAC is an ill-defined line separating the areas controlled by the neighbours and India and China have sparred for decades over this disputed 3,440km (2,100-mile) border. 
China claims Arunachal Pradesh as part of southern Tibet. But Delhi has always rejected the claim, saying the state was an integral part of India. 
The dispute is one of the most persistent challenges inherited by independent India from the British colonial rule in 1947. It led to a brief border war in 1962, in which India suffered a humiliating defeat. 
More than six decades later, much of the frontier remains undemarcated, with the two countries maintaining overlapping territorial claims. 
The region's rugged terrain adds to the challenge: shifting river courses, lakes and snow-covered peaks make it difficult to establish a clear boundary. 
As a result, troops from the two sides can find themselves face-to-face along the frontier, sometimes triggering violent clashes and diplomatic tensions. 
Image source, Anbarasan Ethirajan/BBC Image caption, 
India and China share an ill-defined border demarcated by mountains, rivers and lakes 
The last major escalation came in June 2020 , when Indian and Chinese troops clashed in the Galwan Valley in Ladakh. At least 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese soldiers were killed. 
It was the first fatal confrontation between the two sides since 1975. Indian opposition parties accused the government of losing territory to China - a claim Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government has repeatedly rejected. 
The clashes triggered a sharp deterioration in relations, disrupting diplomatic engagement and affecting trade and travel. After several rounds of negotiations, the neighbours agreed in 2024 to take steps towards easing border tensions. 
They have since moved to restore direct flights and ease visa restrictions imposed after the clashes. 
Chinese President Xi Jinping also visited India in September for the Brics summit, his first visit to the country in seven years. 
These developments raised hopes of a broader normalisation of ties. But the latest reported stand-offs have renewed questions about how much progress has actually been made on the ground. 
After Kapur's comments, the main opposition Congress party once again accused Modi of making concessions to Beijing. 
"The prime minister and his entire apparatus remain silent on this grave issue," senior Congress leader Jairam Ramesh wrote on X , external . 
The Indian government has not explicitly denied Kapur's account that Chinese troops had pitched tents several kilometres inside what India considers to be its side of the LAC. 
Foreign ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal said last week that "the situation in the border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns". 
He said both countries were using military and diplomatic channels to address outstanding issues, but gave no further details. 
A Chinese foreign ministry spokesman said that China had "consistently and strictly adhered to relevant agreements" reached with India and it conducted "normal patrol and management activities in the border areas to safeguard territorial sovereignty". 
Image source, LightRocket via Getty Images Image caption, 
The Galwan clashes were the first fatal confrontation between the two sides since 1975 
Experts say Kapur's remarks offer a rare glimpse into what they describe as China's increasingly assertive military posture along the disputed frontier. 
"This pattern of Chinese probing at various points of the Arunachal Pradesh border has been happening for some time," Shyam Saran, a former Indian foreign secretary who led several rounds of border talks with China in the mid-2000s, told the BBC. 
He said such actions were "not enough to result in an immediate war, but enough to sort of create new facts on the ground". 
Indian opposition parties have long accused China of extending its presence in both Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh, leading to tensions. 
Zhou Bo, a retired senior colonel in China's People's Liberation Army who is now associated with Tsinghua University in Beijing, said both countries had learnt lessons from the 2020 Galwan clashes. 
"The two sides should be more careful to avoid this kind of thing from happening in the future," he said, adding that Chinese media had not reported on the latest stand-offs in Arunachal Pradesh. 
India and China's tensions also come against the backdrop of a complicated economic relationship. 
Despite their differences, the countries remain major trading partners, with bilateral trade , external reaching $151bn last year. But the balance is heavily tilted in Beijing's favour, with Chinese exports to India accounting for about $131bn. 
India continues to rely on Chinese imports for machinery, rare earth magnets, electric vehicle batteries and pharmaceutical products. 
This dependence means tensions with Beijing can have consequences well beyond the border, particularly for Indian industries and infrastructure projects. 
Last week, China also announced restrictions on exports of tunnel-boring machines used in metro rail and highway construction, saying they were intended to protect national security and national interests. Although these curbs were not India specific, they would have a bearing on India's infrastructure push. 
"Chinese policy towards India is designed to complicate India's rise, including India's ability to master certain things in advanced technology and manufacturing," Christopher Clary, a professor at the University at Albany in New York, told the BBC. 
A similar problem emerged last year when China restricted export of rare earth magnets - widely used in electric vehicles, smartphones, wind turbines and medical scanners. 
The move temporarily caused supply problems for Indian industries, highlighting how Beijing's control over key materials can affect global supply chains. 
India is now trying to build domestic capacity to produce rare earth magnets, but developing the industry will take time and investment. 
Image source, Anbarasan Ethirajan/BBC Image caption, 
Arunachal Pradesh has long been the focus of tension between India and China 
For people living along the disputed frontier, the consequences of tensions with China are more immediate. 
"Villagers living in some border areas tell us that they cannot access grazing lands because of Chinese intrusion and encroachment. It's not something new, it's been happening for a long time," says Tongam Rina, a senior journalist with the Arunachal Times. 
This has created a "sense of insecurity among the people here," she adds. 
Villagers usually do not return to those "prohibited" areas for hunting and yak rearing, and they are not sure when they would be allowed again. 
The border dispute also has wider strategic implications for Delhi, with a growing realisation that President Donald Trump's focus on expanding economic engagement with China could limit Washington's willingness to back India in any future confrontation with Beijing. 
China may have little interest in a full-scale conflict with India but, analysts say, it could see advantages in allowing the dispute to continue. 
As China's economic and military power grows, it may calculate that a prolonged stalemate will strengthen its position in any future negotiations. 
For India, the latest stand-offs are a reminder that improved diplomatic ties do not necessarily translate into lasting stability along the border.

articles.title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs
articles.summary: The Villa Vie Odyssey suspended its voyage and is working with passengers on "temporary living arrangements".
articles.full_text:
Image source, Villa Vie Residences Image caption, 
The Villa Vie Odyssey was more than 750 days into its voyage around the world when it came to a stop in Cambodia By Koh Ewe   and   Claire Graham ,  BBC News NI 
- Published 28 October 2026 
A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia. 
The US-based operator of the Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements". 
It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world". 
Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (£6,000) from $1,800. 
Villa Vie Residences said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs". 
"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said. 
The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said. 
There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for Chinese casinos and scam centres. 
The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website. 
Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds. 
The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before announcing its suspension of its journey on Tuesday - which means its passengers would now be stranded in Cambodia. 
Passengers Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin told the BBC they were informed by Villa Vie Residences' chief executive at 6am on Tuesday that they had to leave by 2pm on the same day. 
The couple said passengers had known for some time about the company's financial difficulties. A potential investor had previously come onboard the ship to do due dilligence, but in the end it did not work out. 
"Even then, we were still hoping a miracle investor would come through," they said. "Although there were signs that this would happen, we still felt disbelief when it became real. We were heartbroken. It felt like our dream had been crushed." 
"There have been a lot of hugs and tears as residents support one another and process what has happened." 
Another passenger Holly Hennessey said that the ship's passengers had earlier been asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as global prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed". 
Some people decided to disembark and travel on land, she said. 
"It was not on my bingo card of places where I'd be spending a lot of time," Hennessey told the BBC from Cambodia. 
"We're all in different hotels; there are a number of shipmates in the hotel that I'm in. We're just waiting." 
Canen and Bodin said the location in Cambodia was "a difficult place to disembark" because of the distance to a major international airport. 
Image source, Supplied Image caption, 
Cruise passenger Holly Hennessey and her cat, Captain, have now found themselves in Cambodia 
During their time onboard the Villa Vie Odyssey, passengers had access to several bars and restaurants, a pool deck and a pickleball court, according to its website. 
Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month. 
Last year, the company launched a lifetime residence programme for people to spend their retirement years at sea. 
In 2024, days after US President Donald Trump won his second term, Villa Vie Residences announced a four-year "Skip Forward" package. 
Its CEO told Fox Business at the time that it was the "perfect product for those who said they'd leave the country if 'XYZ' wins the election". 
For Canen and Bodin the experience was "worth it", despite the fact it was shorter than expected. 
"We loved our two years on Odyssey—the adventures, the places we visited and the friends we made along the way." 
Many of the passengers have already made plans to "settle together off the ship, so those friendships and that sense of community are continuing on land", they said. 
The couple plans to spend a few days in Sihanoukville, before travelling to different parts of South East Asia while they "figure out our next chapter". 
But others, like Hennessey, have decided to stick around in Cambodia in the hopes that the Odyssey will set sail again soon. 
"Until they say we are done - done done - I am not giving up. I could never duplicate this lifestyle. The idea of going home? It would be so trite," she said. 
"Cambodia's not the worst place to hang out."

Beijing Queer film festival cancelled after harassment from authorities
Forums for discussion of feminist and LGBTQ+ views face growing intolerance from Chinese state, say experts 
Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities. 
Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals. 
In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.” 
Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood. 
Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues. 
The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues. Film festivals in particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview. 
Beijing Independent film festival, China’s most prominent independent film festival, was closed down in 2014 after the authorities detained the founders and shut off the electricity supply to the venue. Last year, an independent Chinese film festival that was due to be held in New York was cancelled after harassment from the Chinese authorities, an incident which raised concern about transnational repression. 
Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said: “The Chinese government under Xi has been relentlessly tightening social and ideological control, and so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and often also official harassment. 
“The authorities have put more pressure on what little is left of China’s civil society, as well as the LGBT communities and independent film-makers. A queer film festival basically faces all of these overlapping pressures.” 
Hongwei Bao, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of St Andrews who focuses on LGBT issues, said that the festival was “a beacon for LGBT resilience” in China. 
“The shutdown of the Love Queer Cinema Week has a chilling affect on the Chinese queer community,” Bao said. 
In June this year, screenings of films with LGBTQ+ themes that were scheduled to be held in Beijing during Pride month at the Institut Français, a French cultural centre, were cancelled because of police harassment. 
Despite the increased pressure, Beijing Queer film festival remains a popular event. Several international film-makers whose work had been selected for the festival had travelled to China to participate. Last year, the festival received 200 volunteer applications, four times the number received in 2024. 
Beijing’s public security bureau could not be reached for comment.
